parts:
you can try this one. 'constr=2' on generic2 will only sum-to-zero the
second half.

'generic2' is no longer needed as you can do your _0 and the 'trick' at
the end. this was not available at the time generic2 was added



On Thu, 2022-02-17 at 08:19 -0800, Thomas F Johnson wrote:
> Previous code example was incorrect. Here is a better example, with a
> residual, phylogeny, and species precision each set at 1.
>
>
> #Load packages
> library(INLA)
> library(mvtnorm)
> library(ape)
> species_n = 250 #100 species
> tr = rtree(species_n) #Generate a phylogeny for these species
> vcv = vcv.phylo(tr) #And produce a variance-covariance matrix
> prec_mat = solve(vcv) #Convert to a precision matrix
>
> prec_phy = 1 #And overall residual error
> prec_spec = 1 #And overall residual error
> prec_gau = 1 #And overall residual error
>
> trait = rmvnorm(1, mean = rep(prec_phy^-1,species_n), vcv) #Estimate a
> trait value for each species from a MVN()
> phytools::phylosig(tr, trait[1,], method = "lambda")
> trait2 = trait + rnorm(species_n, 0, sqrt(prec_spec^-1))
> phytools::phylosig(tr, trait2[1,], method = "lambda")
>
> #Next, prodcue a dataset describing the above trait value for 100
> individuals of each species
> indiv_n = 10 #With 100 individuals per species
> cmb_df = NULL
> for(a in c(1:species_n)){
>   df = data.frame(
>     species = a,
>     y = trait2[a] + rnorm(indiv_n, 0, sqrt(1 / prec_gau)) #Variance
> between individuals in a species
>   )
>   cmb_df = rbind(cmb_df, df)
> }
> #Add overall residual error
>
> ggplot(cmb_df[c(1:250),]) + #Plot of the first 10 species
>   geom_density(aes(x = y)) +
>   facet_wrap(species~.)
>
> #Run the following model
> pc_prior_gen0 = list(prec = list(prior="pc.prec", param =
> c(sd(cmb_df$y)*3,0.1)))
> cmb_df$phylogeny = cmb_df$species
> m4_0 <- inla(y ~ 1 +
>                f(species, model = "iid", constr = T, hyper =
> pc_prior_gen0) +
>                f(phylogeny, model = "generic0", Cmatrix = prec_mat,
> constr = T, hyper = pc_prior_gen0),
>              data = cmb_df, family = "gaussian",
>              control.inla = list(force.diagonal = T))
> summary(m4_0)
>
> pc_prior_gen2 = list(prec = list(prior="pc.prec", param =
> c(sd(cmb_df$y)*3,0.1)), prec.random = list(prior="pc.prec", param =
> c(sd(cmb_df$y)*3,0.1)))
> m4_2 = inla(y ~
>               f(phylogeny, model = "generic2", Cmatrix = prec_mat,
> constr = T, hyper = pc_prior_gen2),
>             data = cmb_df, family = "gaussian",
>             control.inla = list(force.diagonal = T))
> summary(m4_2)
>
> m4_0$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[1]^-1 #Residual variance model 0
> m4_2$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[1]^-1 #Residual variance model 2
>
> m4_0$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[3]^-1 #Variance captured by the
> phylogeny model 0
> m4_2$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[2]^-1# Variance captured by the
> phylogeny model 2
>
> m4_0$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[2]^-1 #Variance captured by the non-
> phylogenetic effect in model 0 e.g. individual variation
> (phylovar_2/m4_2$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[3]) - phylovar_2
> #Variance captured by the non-phylogenetic effect in model 2 e.g.
> individual variation
>
> m4_2$summary.fixed$sd/m4_0$summary.fixed$sd #SD around intercept is
> nearly 2x larger in the generic2 model
>
>
> On Thursday, 17 February 2022 at 11:15:30 UTC Thomas F Johnson wrote:
> > TLDR: My question - why I am getting such different estimates of the
> > phylogeny and species variances, as well as intercept SD under
> > generic0 and generic2?
> >
> > A common statistical approach to address non-independence in
> > phylogenetic comparative analyses is to use species' shared
> > evolutionary past to specify species covariances.
> >
> > From my understanding, INLAs generic0 and generic2 provide a
> > convenient approach to handle these species covariances using the
> > Cmatrix argument. Imagine a dataset where a trait (e.g. body mass)
> > has been estimated for 100 species, and this trait has high
> > phylogentic signal (traits are more similar in closely related
> > species). Within each species, body mass has been measured for 100
> > individuals, with a within species precision in body mass of 10. See
> > example below
> >
> > #Load packages
> > library(INLA)
> > library(mvtnorm)
> > library(ape)
> > library(ggplot2)
> > set.seed(1)
> > species_n = 100 #100 species
> > tr = rtree(species_n) #Generate a phylogeny for these species
> > vcv = vcv.phylo(tr) #And produce a variance-covariance matrix
> > P = solve(vcv) #Convert to a precision matrix
> > trait = rmvnorm(1, mean = rep(1,species_n), vcv) #Estimate a trait
> > value for each species from a MVN()
> >
> > #Next, prodcue a dataset describing the above trait value for 100
> > individuals of each species
> > indiv_n = 100 #With 100 individuals per species
> > prec_ind = 10 #With a given variance
> > prec_gau = 10 #And overall residual error
> > cmb_df = NULL
> > for(a in c(1:species_n)){
> >   df = data.frame(
> >     species = a,
> >     y = trait[a] + rnorm(indiv_n, 0, sqrt(1 / prec_ind)) #Variance
> > between individuals in a species
> >   )
> >   cmb_df = rbind(cmb_df, df)
> > }
> > cmb_df$y = cmb_df$y + rnorm(nrow(cmb_df), 0, sqrt(1 / prec_gau))
> > #Add overall residual error
> >
> > ggplot(cmb_df[c(1:1000),]) + #Plot of the first 10 species
> >   geom_density(aes(x = y)) +
> >   facet_wrap(species~.)
> >
> > Now, from this dataset, we want to extract the following parameters:
> > the intercept and its variance, as well as the variance captured by
> > the residuals, the phylogenetic covariance matrix, and the non-
> > phylogenetic species effect. To extract these, we could run a model
> > like this:
> >
> > trait ~ intercept + phylogeny + species + residuals
> > phylogeny ~ N(0, tau_phylogenyP) #P represent the precision matrix
> > of relatedness
> > species ~ N(0, tau_species) 
> >
> > Assuming I am correct, I have fit the following model using generic
> > 0 below, with a pc prior:
> >
> > #Run the following model
> > pc_prior_gen0 = list(prec = list(prior="pc.prec", param =
> > c(sd(cmb_df$y)*3,0.1)))
> > cmb_df$phylogeny = cmb_df$species
> > m4_0 <- inla(y ~ 1 +
> >                f(species, model = "iid", constr = T, hyper =
> > pc_prior_gen0) +
> >                f(phylogeny, model = "generic0", Cmatrix = P, constr
> > = T, hyper = pc_prior_gen0),
> >              data = cmb_df, family = "gaussian",
> >              control.inla = list(force.diagonal = T))
> > summary(m4_0)
> >
> > A similar model to above can be fit with generic2, except the
> > species term is dropped as it is included implicitly within the
> > phylogeny term, as species is estimated conditionally on the
> > phylogeny
> >
> > changing from:
> >
> > phylogeny ~ N(0, tau_phylogenyP) #P represent the precision matrix
> > of relatedness
> > species ~ N(0, tau_species) 
> >
> > to:
> > phylogeny ~ N(0, tau_phylogenyP) #P represent the precision matrix
> > of relatedness
> > species ~ N(phylogeny, tau_species) 
> >
> > And in INLA this model would look like:
> >
> > pc_prior_gen2 = list(prec = list(prior="pc.prec", param =
> > c(sd(cmb_df$y)*3,0.1)), prec.random = list(prior="pc.prec", param =
> > c(sd(cmb_df$y)*3,0.1)))
> > m4_2 = inla(y ~
> >               f(phylogeny, model = "generic2", Cmatrix = P, constr =
> > T, hyper = pc_prior_gen2),
> >             data = cmb_df, family = "gaussian",
> >             control.inla = list(force.diagonal = T))
> > summary(m4_2)
> >
> > When you compare the outputs of generic0 and generic2, the residual
> > variance is the same, but the species and phylogeny variance always
> > differ. Further, whilst the intercept is the same, the intercepts
> > standard deviation is normally twice the size in generic2 relative
> > to generic0. See below:
> >
> > m4_0$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[1]^-1 #Residual variance model 0
> > m4_2$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[1]^-1 #Residual variance model 2
> >
> > m4_0$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[3]^-1 #Variance captured by the
> > phylogeny model 0
> > m4_2$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[2]^-1# Variance captured by the
> > phylogeny model 2
> >
> > m4_0$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[2]^-1 #Variance captured by the
> > non-phylogenetic effect in model 0 e.g. individual variation
> > (m4_0$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[2]^-
> > 1/m4_2$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[3]) -
> > m4_0$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[2]^-1 #Variance captured by the
> > non-phylogenetic effect in model 2 e.g. individual variation
> >
> > m4_2$summary.fixed$sd/m4_0$summary.fixed$sd #SD around intercept is
> > nearly 2x larger in the generic2 model
> >
> > My question - why I am getting such different estimates of the
> > phylogeny and species variances, as well as intercept SD under
> > generic0 and generic2?
> >
> > Similar issues have discussed
> > here: https://groups.google.com/g/r-inla-discussion-group/c/wRNZCqqT
> > RVQ/m/jzvR8ufSBAAJ
> >
> > Thanks,
> > Tom
